title: The Cynics: Diogenes and Life Against Convention
subtitle: The man who lived in a jar, mocked Plato and told Alexander the Great to get out of his light
objectives: By the end you will be able to explain why the Hellenistic age turned philosophy toward the question 'How should I live?'
Describe the lives and teachings of Antisthenes, Diogenes, Crates and Hipparchia, separating well-attested facts from legend
Explain the core Cynic ideas: living by nature, self-sufficiency, training, shamelessness, frank speech and cosmopolitanism
Evaluate the strongest objections to Cynicism and trace its influence on the Stoics and on modern thought
hook:
Picture the marketplace of Athens in the middle of the fourth century BCE. Merchants shout, citizens argue about politics, and slaves carry goods between stalls. In the middle of the crowd, an old man with a shaggy beard, a rough cloak and a walking stick is carrying a lit lamp, in broad daylight, peering into people's faces. When someone asks what he is doing, he answers: I am looking for a human being.

The man was Diogenes of Sinope, and the people of Athens called him *kyon*, 'the dog'. From that insult his followers took their name: the **Cynics**, the 'dog-like' philosophers. Diogenes slept in a large clay storage jar, ate and relieved himself in public, begged for his food and insulted the powerful to their faces. Plato, according to one ancient report, called him 'a Socrates gone mad'. Yet for centuries afterwards, serious thinkers saw him as one of the heroes of philosophy. Today we ask why. What was this strange performance for, and does it still have anything to teach a world that is, if anything, even more crowded with conventions than Athens was?

sections.heading: A New World, a New Question
sections.body:
Welcome to Unit 4. For the last three weeks we have been in the world of the Greek city-state, the *polis*, where Socrates questioned his fellow citizens, Plato designed an ideal republic and Aristotle argued, on Day 21, that humans are political animals who flourish only within a city.

That world was changing. In 338 BCE, Philip II of Macedon defeated Athens and Thebes at the battle of Chaeronea. His son Alexander the Great then conquered an empire stretching from Greece to Egypt and the borders of India. When Alexander died in 323 BCE, his generals carved it into rival kingdoms. Historians call the period that follows, until roughly 31 BCE, the **Hellenistic** age, from *Hellen*, 'Greek', because Greek language and culture spread across this vast territory.

Cities like Athens survived, but the real power now lay with distant kings and their armies. Many historians argue that this pushed philosophy in a new direction. If you cannot control your city's fate, the urgent question becomes a personal one: how can *I* live well, and stay free and calm, when so much is beyond my control? Scholars debate how sudden this shift really was, and the Cynics actually began a little before Alexander. But all the great schools of this unit, the Cynics, Epicureans, Stoics and Skeptics, offered something like a medicine for the soul: a complete way of life, not just a set of theories.

The Cynics were the most radical of them. Their answer was simple and shocking. Most of what makes us miserable, they said, is not nature but convention: money, status, manners, reputation and the endless desires that society teaches us to have. Strip all that away, live as simply as an animal, and you will find that you need almost nothing to be happy and free.

sections.heading: Antisthenes: Socrates' Toughest Student
sections.body:
The story usually begins with **Antisthenes** (c. 445–365 BCE). He was a devoted follower of Socrates, and Plato's *Phaedo* names him among the friends present at Socrates' death (Day 10). Ancient sources say he walked several miles into Athens every day to hear Socrates speak.

What Antisthenes admired most in Socrates was not his arguments about definitions but his toughness: his indifference to cold, hunger, money and fear. Socrates walked barefoot in winter, drank without getting drunk and faced death calmly. Antisthenes drew a lesson from this: **virtue is sufficient for happiness**. You need nothing else, not wealth, not honour, not even good luck, provided you have the strength of character Socrates had. And virtue, he held, is shown more in deeds than in words, and can be taught.

Antisthenes taught at a gymnasium called the Cynosarges, and some ancient writers thought the name 'Cynic' came from there rather than from the word for dog. Later tradition, especially the biographer Diogenes Laertius, made Antisthenes the founder of Cynicism and Diogenes his pupil. Modern scholars are more cautious. The dates fit awkwardly, and Antisthenes lived a fairly conventional life compared with Diogenes. A common view today is that Antisthenes supplied the ideas and Diogenes invented the Cynic way of life.

Either way, the line of descent matters. It runs from Socrates through the Cynics to the Stoics, whom you will meet on Day 25. Each step makes the Socratic idea that virtue is what really matters more radical.

sections.heading: Diogenes: The Dog of Athens
sections.body:
Before we meet **Diogenes of Sinope** (c. 412/404–323 BCE), a warning. He left no writings that survive. Ancient lists credit him with dialogues, tragedies and a *Republic*, but they are lost. Almost everything we know comes from collections of anecdotes and sayings, above all Book 6 of Diogenes Laertius's *Lives of the Eminent Philosophers*, written around five hundred years later. Many of these stories are surely legends, polished and retold because they were funny or pointed. Read them as portraits of the Cynic ideal, not as reliable reporting.

Diogenes came from Sinope, a Greek city on the southern shore of the Black Sea. His father was a banker or money-changer, and Diogenes was involved in some scandal about **defacing the currency**, probably adulterating or cutting coins. Coins minted at Sinope in this period have been found deliberately defaced, which suggests the story has a real basis. He was exiled and made his way to Athens. The ancient tradition adds that an oracle had told him to 'deface the currency', and that he later understood this as a mission. The Greek word *nomisma*, coin, is closely related to *nomos*, custom or law. Diogenes would devote his life to defacing the currency of convention: exposing society's values as counterfeit.

The famous stories follow from this mission.

- He lived in a *pithos*, a large clay storage jar, in the city. (It was not a wooden barrel, as later paintings show; barrels were not yet common in Greece.)
- He owned a cloak, a staff, a bag and a cup. Seeing a child drink water from cupped hands, he threw away his cup, saying a child had beaten him in simplicity.
- When Plato defined a human being as a 'featherless biped', Diogenes is said to have plucked a chicken, brought it to the Academy and announced: here is Plato's human being. Plato, the story goes, added 'with broad flat nails' to the definition.
- Asked where he came from, he said he was a **citizen of the world**.

The most famous story of all is his meeting with Alexander the Great, reported by Plutarch and others. Alexander, at the height of his power, found Diogenes sunning himself in Corinth and offered to grant him anything he wished. Diogenes replied: stand a little out of my sun. Alexander is supposed to have remarked that if he were not Alexander, he would wish to be Diogenes. Scholars doubt the meeting ever happened. But notice how perfectly it makes the Cynic point. The most powerful man in the world has nothing to give the man who wants nothing.

Diogenes died in Corinth around 323 BCE, according to one tradition on the very same day as Alexander. That coincidence is almost certainly another legend.

sections.heading: Living According to Nature
sections.body:
Behind the jokes lies a serious philosophy. Remember the debate on Day 8 between *nomos*, human convention, and *physis*, nature? Some Sophists used it to argue that justice is merely conventional and that the strong should take what they can. The Cynics used it differently. They agreed that most social rules are mere convention, but concluded that a wise person should ignore them and live **according to nature** (*kata physin*).

What does nature require? Very little: food, water, shelter from the worst weather. Diogenes is said to have been inspired by watching a mouse scurry about, not looking for a bed, not afraid of the dark and not wanting any of the so-called luxuries. Animals, and especially dogs, became Cynic role models. A dog eats when it is hungry, sleeps where it is tired, is loyal to friends and barks at enemies. It has no idea what the neighbours think.

From this followed several key Cynic ideas.

1. **Autarkeia**, self-sufficiency. The fewer things you need, the less anyone can take from you or control you with. Diogenes reportedly said it was the privilege of the gods to need nothing, and of god-like people to need very little.
2. **Askesis**, training. Freedom has to be practised, like athletics. Diogenes is said to have rolled in hot sand in summer and hugged snow-covered statues in winter to harden himself. He begged from statues, he explained, to get used to being refused. Our word *ascetic* comes from *askesis*.
3. **Ponos**, toil or hardship, is good for you, while easy pleasure softens you. The Cynics liked the hero Heracles, who won his fame through labours rather than comfort.
4. **Anaideia**, shamelessness. If an act is not wrong in itself, it is not wrong to do it in public. Diogenes ate in the marketplace, which respectable Greeks did not do, and performed even more private bodily acts in public. The point was to show that our sense of shame often tracks custom, not genuine wrongdoing.
5. **Parrhesia**, frank speech. The Cynic says exactly what he thinks to anyone, including kings. Asked what was the finest thing among human beings, Diogenes reportedly answered: frank speech.

Put together, these make Cynicism less a set of doctrines than a demonstration. The Cynic's own life was the argument. Every shocking act asked onlookers a Socratic question: why do you think this matters? Who told you so?

sections.heading: Crates and Hipparchia: Cynicism with a Smile
sections.body:
Diogenes was famously harsh. His most important follower showed that Cynicism could also be gentle. **Crates of Thebes** (c. 365–285 BCE) was born rich. After encountering Cynic ideas, he gave away his fortune and took up the cloak and the bag. Yet the stories about him are warm. He was nicknamed the 'Door-Opener' because he would walk into people's houses uninvited to give advice, and people apparently welcomed him. He wrote witty poems, including a parody describing an imaginary island city called Pera, which is Greek for the beggar's bag, where no one fights over money or glory.

Crates' wife was **Hipparchia** of Maroneia, one of the few women philosophers of antiquity whose story we have. Born into a wealthy family, she fell in love with Crates and his way of life and threatened to kill herself if her parents did not let her marry him. Crates, the story goes, stood before her, took off his cloak, and said: this is the bridegroom, and these are his possessions; choose accordingly. She chose him and lived as a Cynic, wearing the same clothes as Crates and going with him to dinners where women were not normally present.

Diogenes Laertius reports her exchange with a philosopher named Theodorus, who mocked her for abandoning the loom. She replied that she was not wrong to spend on her education the time she would otherwise have spent at weaving. For a woman in fourth-century Greece, that was a radical claim. Cynicism, by rejecting convention wholesale, opened a door that most philosophical schools kept shut.

Crates matters for another reason too. One of his students was a young merchant from Cyprus named Zeno. Zeno would go on to found Stoicism (Day 25), and the Stoics always honoured the Cynics as an important part of their own ancestry, even as they softened Cynic shamelessness into something more respectable.

sections.heading: Was Diogenes Right? Objections and Legacy
sections.body:
Cynicism raises sharp objections, and ancient critics raised most of them.

First, the **free-rider problem**. Diogenes rejected society, yet he lived in a city, drank from its fountains and begged food from people who worked for a living. If everyone lived as he did, who would grow the grain? The Cynic might reply that he never asked everyone to become a beggar, only to stop overvaluing wealth. But the dependence is real.

Second, is all convention really bad? Aristotle (Day 21) would say that humans are political animals and that law, language and manners are not chains but part of our nature as social, speaking beings. Some conventions, such as driving on one side of the road, help everyone. Others protect the vulnerable. A blanket rejection of convention throws out the useful with the oppressive.

Third, there is the question of whether shocking behaviour persuades anyone or merely entertains. The Cynics were admired, but they were also treated as a kind of street theatre. A performance can easily become self-indulgence.

Still, the Cynics' influence was enormous. The Stoics took over their ideas of living according to nature, of virtue as the only true good and of world citizenship. In Roman times, wandering Cynics in rough cloaks were a familiar sight; the Stoic Epictetus (Day 26) painted a noble portrait of the true Cynic as a messenger sent by god to show people their errors. Some scholars have compared the wandering, possession-free preachers of the early Christian movement to Cynic teachers, though how close the link is remains debated.

Finally, notice what has happened to the word. A 'cynic' today is someone who distrusts everyone's motives and believes in nothing. That is almost the opposite of Diogenes, who believed passionately in virtue and freedom and mocked others precisely because he thought they could live better. The ancient Cynic was not a sneering pessimist but a disappointed idealist with a lamp.

keyQuote.text: I am a citizen of the world.
keyQuote.source: Diogenes of Sinope, as reported by Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Eminent Philosophers 6.63

modernConnection.title: Minimalists, Pranksters and the Courage of Truth
modernConnection.body:
The Cynics have unexpected heirs today. Consider the minimalism movement: people who declutter their homes, own a hundred things or fewer, live in tiny houses or vans, and argue that consumer culture sells us desires we never needed. Diogenes throwing away his cup is the founding image of this impulse. Psychologists have also found that people who strongly prioritise money, image and status, what researchers like Tim Kasser call materialistic values, tend on average to report lower well-being. That is a Cynic conclusion reached with questionnaires.

But the comparison has a twist the Cynics would have loved. Much modern minimalism is itself a consumer product: beautifully photographed empty rooms, expensive 'simple' furniture and books and courses about owning less. Diogenes would ask whether this is freedom from convention or just a new convention with better lighting. A real Cynic test is not how your apartment looks but whether you could lose your possessions and your reputation without losing your peace.

The Cynic tradition of performance protest is also alive. Activists who stage street theatre, artists who mock the powerful, and comedians who say what politicians will not are all practising a kind of *parrhesia*, frank speech that takes a personal risk. The French philosopher Michel Foucault devoted his final lecture course, *The Courage of Truth* (1984), to the Cynics, arguing that they made their very lives into a public, scandalous form of truth-telling.

Where does the comparison break down? Online shock culture often borrows Cynic shamelessness without Cynic purpose. Trolling, outrage bait and provocation for clicks mimic Diogenes' rudeness, but Diogenes risked poverty, exile and contempt for the sake of a message about virtue, whereas the troll usually risks nothing and wants attention, which is exactly the kind of reputation-chasing the Cynics despised. The question to ask of any provocateur is the Cynic one: what convention are you exposing, and what are you giving up to do it?

vocabulary.definition: From the Greek kyon, 'dog': a follower of the philosophical way of life associated with Diogenes, which rejected convention in favour of a simple life according to nature. Not the same as the modern meaning of a person who distrusts everyone's motives.
vocabulary.example: The ancient Cynic owned only a cloak, a staff and a bag, and believed that this made him freer than any king.

vocabulary.definition: The period of Greek culture from the death of Alexander the Great in 323 BCE to roughly 31 BCE, when Greek language and ideas spread across the kingdoms carved from his empire.
vocabulary.example: The Cynics, Epicureans, Stoics and Skeptics are the great philosophical schools of the Hellenistic age.

vocabulary.definition: The condition of needing as little as possible from outside yourself, so that no person or misfortune can control you.
vocabulary.example: By reducing his needs to bread, water and a cloak, Diogenes aimed at complete autarkeia.

vocabulary.definition: Deliberate practice and self-discipline undertaken to build the strength needed for a virtuous, free life; the root of the English word 'ascetic'.
vocabulary.example: Taking a cold shower to prove to yourself that discomfort is bearable is a small modern form of askesis.

vocabulary.definition: The Cynic practice of openly doing in public things that are not wrong in themselves but that convention says should be hidden, in order to expose custom as arbitrary.
vocabulary.example: Eating in the Athenian marketplace, which respectable people avoided, was a deliberate act of Cynic anaideia.

vocabulary.definition: Speaking the truth openly and boldly, especially to the powerful and at personal risk.
vocabulary.example: Telling Alexander the Great to step out of his sunlight was a legendary act of parrhesia.

vocabulary.definition: From kosmopolites, 'citizen of the world': the view that one's deepest loyalty is to humanity as a whole rather than to a particular city or nation.
vocabulary.example: Diogenes' claim to be a citizen of the world is the earliest recorded expression of cosmopolitanism.

vocabulary.definition: Convention (human custom and law) versus nature; the Cynics held that most of what makes people unhappy belongs to nomos, and that we should live by physis.
vocabulary.example: For a Cynic, the need to drink is physis, but the need to drink from a silver cup is merely nomos.

thinkingExercise.title: Deface Your Own Currency
thinkingExercise.prompt: Diogenes believed that many of the values we take for granted are counterfeit coins minted by convention. Spend 10 to 15 minutes testing some of your own.
steps: List five things you spent money, time or worry on in the past week (for example a new phone case, a haircut, answering messages quickly, what to wear to an event).
For each one, ask the Cynic question: is this a need of nature or a demand of convention? Mark each N, C or 'a bit of both'.
Pick one item marked C. Imagine giving it up for a month. What exactly would you lose? What would you fear people would think?
Now play Aristotle's advocate: write two or three sentences defending one convention on your list as genuinely valuable for a social, political animal.
Conclude: where would you draw the line between conventions worth keeping and conventions worth defacing? Write your rule in one sentence.

summary: The Hellenistic age, after Alexander's conquests, turned philosophy toward the personal question of how to live well and freely in a world one cannot control.
Antisthenes, a follower of Socrates, held that virtue is sufficient for happiness; Diogenes of Sinope turned this into a radical, public way of life.
The Cynics rejected convention (nomos) and tried to live according to nature (physis), aiming at self-sufficiency through training, shamelessness and frank speech.
Most stories about Diogenes, including his meeting with Alexander, come from much later anecdote collections and are probably legendary, but they capture the Cynic ideal.
Crates and Hipparchia showed a gentler Cynicism, and Crates' student Zeno went on to found Stoicism, which inherited cosmopolitanism and the idea of living by nature.
Ancient Cynics were idealists, not 'cynics' in the modern sense; critics rightly ask whether they depended on the society they rejected and whether all convention is bad.

quiz.question: Where does the name 'Cynic' most likely come from?
options: From the city of Sinope, where Diogenes was born
From the Greek word for 'doubt'
From kyon, the Greek word for 'dog', an insult applied to Diogenes
From a book called the Cynica written by Plato
quiz.explanation: Diogenes was nicknamed 'the dog' for his shameless, animal-like life, and his followers adopted the label. Some ancients also linked the name to the Cynosarges gymnasium where Antisthenes taught.

quiz.question: What lesson did Antisthenes take above all from Socrates?
options: That virtue is sufficient for happiness and is shown in a tough, self-controlled life
That the Forms exist in a separate world
That pleasure is the highest good
That we can know nothing and should suspend judgment
quiz.explanation: Antisthenes admired Socrates' endurance and indifference to wealth and comfort, and concluded that virtue alone is enough for happiness, the seed of Cynic and later Stoic ethics.

quiz.question: Diogenes was involved in 'defacing the currency' at Sinope. How did the Cynic tradition reinterpret this phrase?
options: As a call to abolish money and introduce barter
As a mission to expose society's customs and values as counterfeit
As a reference to a statue Diogenes destroyed
As a metaphor for teaching mathematics
quiz.explanation: The Greek for coin (nomisma) is linked to nomos, custom. Diogenes' life became an attempt to 'deface' conventional values, showing they were not genuinely valuable.

quiz.question: Which of these is the best example of Cynic askesis?
options: Writing a long treatise on the nature of virtue
Buying an expensive cloak to look like a philosopher
Voting in the Athenian assembly
Hugging a snow-covered statue to get used to cold
quiz.explanation: Askesis means training: deliberately practising hardship so that comfort and luck lose their grip on you. Diogenes' reported winter statue-hugging is a classic example.

quiz.question: A comedian on live television mocks a powerful politician who is sitting in the audience, knowing it may cost her future bookings. Which Cynic idea does this best illustrate?
options: Autarkeia
Parrhesia
Ataraxia
Physis
quiz.explanation: Parrhesia is frank, risky speech to the powerful. Diogenes is reported to have called it the finest thing among humans.

quiz.question: Why do historians treat the story of Diogenes and Alexander with caution?
options: Because Diogenes and Alexander lived in different centuries
Because Diogenes wrote a version of it himself that contradicts Plutarch
Because it comes from anecdote collections written long afterward and fits the Cynic message almost too perfectly
Because Alexander never visited Corinth
quiz.explanation: The two were contemporaries, but the story survives in later sources such as Plutarch and Diogenes Laertius, and many such anecdotes were polished or invented to illustrate the Cynic ideal.

quiz.question: Which of the following is a strong objection to the Cynic way of life?
options: Cynics depended on the very society whose conventions they rejected, for example by begging
Cynics were too wealthy to understand ordinary people
Cynics refused to speak to anyone in public
Cynics believed that only the gods could be happy
quiz.explanation: This is the free-rider objection: Diogenes drank from city fountains and begged from people who worked, so his independence was partly made possible by others' conventional lives.

quiz.question: According to the ancient sources, Hipparchia adopted the Cynic way of life alongside her husband Crates and defended a woman's right to spend her time on education.
quiz.explanation: Diogenes Laertius reports her marriage to Crates, her Cynic dress and lifestyle, and her reply to Theodorus defending her choice of education over weaving.

quiz.question: The ancient Cynics were 'cynical' in the modern sense: they believed nothing was truly worth caring about.
quiz.explanation: Ancient Cynics passionately valued virtue and freedom. They attacked convention because they believed people could live far better, which is closer to idealism than to modern cynicism.

quiz.question: Zeno of Citium, the founder of Stoicism, studied with the Cynic Crates.
quiz.explanation: Zeno was Crates' student, and the Stoics inherited key Cynic ideas such as living according to nature and world citizenship, as you will see on Day 25.

goDeeper.body:
Was Cynicism a philosophy at all, or just a lifestyle? The ancients themselves argued about it. Some said Cynicism was a genuine school with doctrines; others called it merely a 'way of life' or, in a famous phrase, a 'short cut to virtue'. Modern scholars have revived the debate. Because Diogenes' own writings are lost, we cannot tell how much theory lay behind the performances. Some, like Luis Navia, read him as a systematic critic of civilisation; others stress that the anecdote tradition built a literary character who may differ from the historical man.

A striking modern line of interpretation comes from Michel Foucault, whose final lectures at the Collège de France in 1984, published as *The Courage of Truth*, presented the Cynics as the purest practitioners of parrhesia. For Foucault, the Cynic did not just speak truth but made his whole existence a visible test of truth, a 'true life' that challenged everyone who saw it. The German philosopher Peter Sloterdijk, in *Critique of Cynical Reason* (1983), drew a different contrast. He distinguished ancient 'kynicism', the cheeky, embodied protest of Diogenes from below, from modern 'cynicism', the knowing, defeated attitude of people who see through the system's lies and go along with it anyway.

The Cynic idea of world citizenship also has a long future. You will see the Stoics turn it into a positive picture of humanity as one community bound by reason, and Kant (Day 57) develop a 'cosmopolitan' right in his essay on perpetual peace. Contemporary philosophers such as Martha Nussbaum and Kwame Anthony Appiah continue the debate about whether our deepest loyalties belong to humanity or to our particular communities.

readings.title: Lives of the Eminent Philosophers, Book 6
readings.author: Diogenes Laertius
readings.note: The main ancient source for Antisthenes, Diogenes, Crates and Hipparchia. Short, lively and often very funny; the 2018 Oxford translation by Pamela Mensch, edited by James Miller, is beautifully illustrated.

readings.title: Diogenes the Cynic: Sayings and Anecdotes, with Other Popular Moralists
readings.author: Robin Hard (translator)
readings.note: An Oxford World's Classics collection that gathers the scattered stories and sayings in one place, with helpful notes.

readings.title: The Cynics: The Cynic Movement in Antiquity and Its Legacy
readings.author: R. Bracht Branham and Marie-Odile Goulet-Cazé (editors)
readings.note: A scholarly but accessible collection of essays on the ancient Cynics and their afterlife, from Christianity to the Renaissance.

readings.title: The Courage of Truth
readings.author: Michel Foucault
readings.note: For the ambitious: his last lecture course, with extended discussion of Cynic parrhesia and the 'true life'.

questions: Can shocking or offensive behaviour ever be the best way to make a philosophical point? Where is the line between Cynic parrhesia and simple rudeness?
Is it possible to reject the conventions of your society while still depending on it? Does that dependence undermine the Cynic's message?
Is 'citizen of the world' a meaningful identity, or do we need particular communities, as Aristotle argued?
